## --------------  -----  --------  ----------  -------  --------
## IC50             3237      2353   36078.751     0.00   3.0e+07
## Ki               1480       920    5952.212     0.15   1.0e+05
## Kd                346        63   23149.319     0.28   4.7e+05
num <- c("n", "n_exact", "mean_nM", "min_nM", "max_nM")
cat("\nidentical shape:", identical(dim(sql_answer), dim(dplyr_answer)),
    "| identical keys:", identical(sql_answer$standard_type, dplyr_answer$standard_type),
    "| identical values:",
    all(abs(as.matrix(sql_answer[num]) - as.matrix(dplyr_answer[num])) < 1e-3), "\n")
## 
## identical shape: TRUE | identical keys: TRUE | identical values: TRUE
cat(sprintf("timing on this table: SQL %.1f ms vs dplyr %.1f ms\n", t_sql * 1000, t_dplyr * 1000))
## timing on this table: SQL 2.0 ms vs dplyr 5.0 ms
cat("maximum absolute difference across the compared columns:",
    max(abs(as.matrix(sql_answer[num]) - as.matrix(dplyr_answer[num]))), "\n")
## maximum absolute difference across the compared columns: 0
cmp <- rbind(data.frame(type = sql_answer$standard_type, n = sql_answer$n, system = "SQL"),
             data.frame(type = dplyr_answer$standard_type, n = dplyr_answer$n, system = "dplyr"))
p1 <- ggplot(cmp, aes(type, n, fill = system)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format(n, big.mark = ",")), position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(SQL = PAL[["blue"]], dplyr = "#a8c6e6")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.14))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "records with a value", fill = NULL, title = "Same counts from both systems") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p2 <- ggplot(data.frame(system = c("SQL", "dplyr"), ms = c(t_sql, t_dplyr) * 1000),
             aes(system, ms, fill = system)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f ms", ms)), vjust = -0.3, size = 2.9, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(SQL = PAL[["blue"]], dplyr = "#a8c6e6")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.16))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "time for the whole query (ms)", title = "and comparable cost on this table")
print(p1 | p2)

Figure 8. Left: the record count per measurement type as computed by SQL (dark) and by dplyr (light) — the bars are identical, which is the verification the syllabus asks for, and the printed maximum absolute difference across the compared columns is zero to rounding. Right: the wall-clock cost of each implementation on this in-memory-sized table. Neither system is “the fast one”; what differs is where the data already are and how the question is phrased.

The two answers agree on every key and every value to three decimals — which is the point of the exercise. SQL and dplyr are two syntaxes for the same relational operations, and the choice between them is pragmatic: SQL when the data live in a database, when the query joins several tables, or when the table does not fit in memory; dplyr when the data are already loaded, when the operation is not expressible relationally (a bootstrap, a model fit, a plot), or when it is one step of a longer R pipeline. The timing printed above is for one table that fits comfortably in memory, where the difference is of no consequence — and a measurement, not a general claim. R offers a third option worth knowing: dbplyr lets you write dplyr verbs against a database connection and translates them to SQL, so the same pipeline can run in R or in the database by changing where the data come from.

Exercise 2

Write the SQL that answers: “for each assay type, how many distinct compounds have at least two exactly-measured IC50 records in different documents?” You will need a subquery, a GROUP BY with HAVING, and a join to assays. Then write the dplyr equivalent and compare the two results as above. Finally, add an index on activities(standard_type, standard_relation) and re-time your query: does it help, and why does an index on a column with three distinct values help less than an index on a compound identifier? For the last part, run the same pipeline through dbplyr (tbl(con, “activities”) |> group_by(…) |> summarise(…)) and inspect the generated SQL with show_query().

7. Terms of use, licences and when scraping is not acceptable

Three obligations attach to data you did not generate, and all three are part of the method rather than of the paperwork.

The licence governs redistribution. ChEMBL is CC BY-SA 3.0, so a derived table must carry the same licence (Unit 2); PubChem’s own content is public domain, but individual depositor submissions may carry their own terms; the PDB is open; GEO data are public but the associated publications are not. Record the licence of every source in your manifest before building a derived table.

The terms of use govern access. Public APIs publish rate limits and acceptable-use policies. NCBI, for instance, limits anonymous E-utilities requests and asks for an identifying tool name and contact address — which is why the client in Section 4 sets a user agent. Exceeding the limits gets your institution’s address blocked, which affects your colleagues, not only you.

robots.txt governs crawling. A web server publishes /robots.txt to declare which paths automated clients may fetch; the format is standardised as RFC 9309[29]. R has no parser for it in the environment that builds these pages — Python’s standard library has one, which the Python edition uses — so the next chunk implements the subset that matters in a dozen lines, which is itself instructive: the format is small enough that there is no excuse for not checking.

## Parsing a robots.txt policy (text written in-chunk, not fetched) and honouring it.
policy <- c("User-agent: *", "Disallow: /private/", "Disallow: /cgi-bin/", "Crawl-delay: 5",
            "", "User-agent: GreedyBot", "Disallow: /")
writeLines(policy, file.path(SCRATCH, "robots.txt"))

parse_robots <- function(lines) {
  groups <- list(); agents <- character(0); rules <- list(); delay <- NA_real_
  flush <- function() if (length(agents))
    for (a in agents) groups[[a]] <<- list(rules = rules, delay = delay)
  for (ln in c(lines, "")) {
    ln <- trimws(sub("#.*", "", ln))
    if (!nzchar(ln)) { flush(); agents <- character(0); rules <- list(); delay <- NA_real_; next }
    kv <- strsplit(ln, ":", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
    key <- tolower(trimws(kv[1])); value <- trimws(paste(kv[-1], collapse = ":"))
    if (key == "user-agent") agents <- c(agents, value)
    else if (key %in% c("disallow", "allow")) rules[[length(rules) + 1]] <- list(key, value)
    else if (key == "crawl-delay") delay <- as.numeric(value)
  }
  flush(); groups
}
can_fetch <- function(groups, agent, path) {
  g <- groups[[agent]]; if (is.null(g)) g <- groups[["*"]]
  if (is.null(g)) return(TRUE)
  allowed <- TRUE
  for (r in g$rules) {
    if (nzchar(r[[2]]) && startsWith(path, r[[2]])) allowed <- (r[[1]] == "allow")
  }
  allowed
}

groups <- parse_robots(policy)
tests <- list(c("*", "/data/activities.csv"), c("*", "/private/internal.csv"),
              c("*", "/cgi-bin/query"), c("GreedyBot", "/data/activities.csv"))
for (t in tests)
  cat(sprintf("  %-10s https://example.org%-30s -> %s\n", t[1], t[2],
              if (can_fetch(groups, t[1], t[2])) "allowed" else "DISALLOWED"))
##   *          https://example.org/data/activities.csv           -> allowed
##   *          https://example.org/private/internal.csv          -> DISALLOWED
##   *          https://example.org/cgi-bin/query                 -> DISALLOWED
##   GreedyBot  https://example.org/data/activities.csv           -> DISALLOWED
cat("\ncrawl delay requested for a generic client:", groups[["*"]]$delay, "seconds\n")
## 
## crawl delay requested for a generic client: 5 seconds
cat("groups parsed:", paste(names(groups), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## groups parsed: *, GreedyBot
cat("\nAnd the rule no file can express: if a bulk download or an API exists, use it instead.\n")
## 
## And the rule no file can express: if a bulk download or an API exists, use it instead.

The parser answers per user agent and per path, and it reports the requested crawl delay — which a polite client sleeps for between requests. Our twelve-line version implements prefix matching and “last matching rule wins”; the real standard adds wildcards, $ anchoring and a longest-match rule, so use a maintained implementation in production. But the decisive judgement is not technical. Scraping is not acceptable when an API or a bulk download exists (you are generating load for no reason), when the terms of use forbid it, when the content is behind authentication or a paywall, when the data are personal, or when your crawl would degrade a service other researchers depend on. In this laboratory, the order of preference is always: bulk download, then official API client, then hand-written API calls, and scraping only for a page that exists nowhere else — after asking.

## Close the database and remove every temporary artefact.
dbDisconnect(con)
unlink(SCRATCH, recursive = TRUE, force = TRUE)
cat("scratch directory removed:", !dir.exists(SCRATCH), "\n")
## scratch directory removed: TRUE
cat("the frozen tables in ../data/ were read, never modified:",
    file.exists(data_path("rock1_chembl_raw.csv")), "\n")
## the frozen tables in ../data/ were read, never modified: TRUE

Bridge — where the data go next

This unit filled data/raw/. Unit 2 is what makes its downloads citable: manifest, checksum, licence, DOI; Unit 1 built the project layout they land in. The later units of this R edition follow the sequence of the Python edition, whose counterparts already exist: tidy data reshapes what arrived into a tidy table[30] — one row per observation, one column per variable — and data quality curates it into the modelling table used from Unit 7 onwards, with a logged decision for every record it removes. Sequence and omics data returns to FASTA and GEO, molecular-dynamics analytics to trajectory formats, and software engineering turns the API client of Section 4 into a tested, installable package. In the sister courses, the cheminformatics elective covers SMILES and InChI and chemical databases in chemical depth, while BGM324 shows what is done with the structures retrieved from the PDB in structure prediction and docking, and the R edition of BGM411 (study material) reads the same tables into its model code.

8. Summary

You should now be able to explain, without notes:

  • The four axes along which file formats differ, and which format this group uses for raw downloads, intermediate tables, large numeric arrays and nested metadata — with the measurement that justifies each choice, and why RDS is right for a fitted model and wrong for an exchanged table.
  • Exactly what a CSV loses, which kinds of value do not survive a round trip in R, and the three fread arguments that defend against it — including the one whose default destroys a column containing the literal text NA.
  • Why a columnar format reads the same table an order of magnitude faster than a CSV, and why fread’s select = nevertheless gains proportionally as much — it skips column construction, not the scan.
  • What SMILES, SDF, FASTA and PDB/mmCIF each store, how a fixed-column format is parsed with substr(), and why splitting a PDB line on whitespace is a bug that passes its first test.
  • The anatomy of an HTTP request, the meaning of the status codes that matter, and the four disciplines of a well-behaved client: timeout, pagination, backoff with jitter, cache — plus the user agent that lets an administrator contact you instead of blocking you.
  • Why a live call must always print its own provenance, and why this course’s documents read frozen files.
  • The identifier systems of the field, the three blocks of an InChIKey, and how many structures in this course’s own table would be merged by deduplicating on the skeleton block.
  • What row inflation is, how a non-unique join key changes a mean, and the three defences against it — one of which data.table enforces for you.
  • The relational model in three sentences; SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, subqueries; why NULL comparisons are never true; and the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) on a left join.
  • When a database beats a folder of CSV files, what an index costs and buys, and what setkey() is the in-memory equivalent of.
  • The licence, terms-of-use and robots.txt obligations, and the order of preference: bulk download, official client, hand-written calls, and scraping only as a last resort after asking.

9. Self-assessment

Q1. A collaborator sends a CSV in which a compound identifier column has lost its leading zeros and a comment column has become empty. Explain both, and give the fread call that would have prevented them.

CSV stores characters, not types, so the reader inferred an integer type for the identifier column (dropping leading zeros) and treated the literal string NA as missing, because fread’s default na.strings includes it. Prevent both with explicit arguments: fread(path, colClasses = c(plate_well = “character”), na.strings = ““). Better still, exchange the file as Parquet, which carries a schema and round-trips exactly.

Q2. Restricting a read to two of twenty-five columns speeds up both fread and read_parquet. Does that mean the columnar layout buys nothing?

No — it means the two readers save different things. Parquet stores each column as a separate compressed block with its own metadata, so it seeks to two blocks and never touches the rest of the file; its absolute times are an order of magnitude lower than the CSV reader’s, on a file a hundred times smaller. fread must still scan every byte to locate the separators, but that multi-threaded scan is not where its time goes: allocating and type-converting twenty-five columns, several of them long strings, is, and select = skips exactly that. Hence a similar ratio from a much worse baseline. The measured times are printed in Section 2.

Q3. You must store a 2048-bit fingerprint for ten million molecules. Which format, and why not CSV?

A binary array format — HDF5, or a sparse matrix written as Parquet — because the data are a homogeneous numeric matrix, and because a CSV would store each bit as a character plus a separator, inflating the file by an order of magnitude and making every read a parse. A sparse representation is better still when most bits are zero, which is why this course’s frozen fingerprint files store only the set bits as (id, bit) pairs.

Q4. Which HTTP status codes should a client retry, which should it never retry, and why does the backoff need jitter?

Retry 429 and 5xx (transient: rate limit or server failure). Never retry 400, 401, 403 or 404 — the request itself is wrong, so repeating it only adds load. Jitter decorrelates the retries of many clients that failed at the same moment, preventing a synchronised second wave that would knock the service over again.

Q5. This document calls a live API but its results are reproducible. How?

Because the live call is wrapped in tryCatch() with a timeout, its result is cached, its provenance is printed, and every number used downstream comes from the frozen, checksummed file in ../data/. The network call serves to date the snapshot — comparing the live record count with the frozen one — not to produce the analysis. Note also req_error(is_error = function(resp) FALSE), which stops httr2 from raising on a 4xx or 5xx so that the chunk can report the status rather than abort the knit.

Q6. Two molecules share the first 14 characters of their InChIKey. What do you know, and what must you not conclude?

You know they have the same constitutional skeleton — the same atoms connected in the same way. You must not conclude they are the same compound: the second block encodes stereochemistry and isotopes, so enantiomers and diastereomers share the skeleton block while differing pharmacologically, and the final character encodes protonation state. Section 5 counted how many such collisions exist in this course’s own curated table; match on the full key.

Q7. After a merge, your table has more rows than the left table and the mean of a value column has changed. What happened, and what are the three defences?

The join key was not unique on the right-hand side, so matching rows were duplicated (row inflation), and duplicated rows now contribute multiple times to the mean. Defences: assert the row count after the merge; check uniqueN(key) == nrow(tbl) on the side that must be unique before merging; and leave data.table’s allow.cartesian = FALSE default in place so that it stops you. In dplyr, relationship = “many-to-one” plays the same role.

Q8. Why does WHERE standard_value = NULL return no rows, and what is the correct clause?

Because NULL represents the absence of a value, and any comparison with it evaluates to NULL, which is not TRUE, so no row satisfies the condition. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. The same logic explains why NULL rows vanish from inner joins and why aggregate functions ignore them — and it is the same reason R requires is.na(x) rather than x == NA.

Q9. On a left join of compounds to activities, COUNT(*) reports 1 for a compound with no measurements. Why, and which function should you use?

The left join produced one row for that compound with NULL in the activity columns, and COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of content. COUNT(activity_id) ignores NULLs and correctly reports 0. This is the hand-traced result of Section 6.1, confirmed in SQL and in dplyr, where the equivalent pair is n() and sum(!is.na(activity_id)).

Q10. When is a database the right tool, and when is data.table?

A database when the data are queried repeatedly by key, when they exceed memory, when several processes read them concurrently, or when types and constraints must be enforced; an index then turns scans into lookups (Figure 7). data.table when the table fits in memory and the work is a single pass, or when the operation is not relational — fitting a model, bootstrapping, plotting; setkey() gives it the same lookup advantage in memory. The two are not rivals: load with SQL, analyse in R, and use dbplyr when you want one pipeline to serve both.

Q11. A website has the data you need and no API. List, in order, what you do.

  1. Look for a bulk download or an official client — most large resources publish one. (2) Read the terms of use and robots.txt; check whether your paths are allowed and what crawl delay is requested. (3) Ask the data owner; a polite email often returns a file. (4) Only then consider a rate-limited, cached, identified crawl of the permitted paths — and never for personal data, paywalled content, or a service that would be degraded by it.

Q12. The live record count for the target differs from the frozen snapshot’s. Is something wrong?

Not necessarily, and there are two innocent explanations before any guilty one. A curated, versioned database releases new content twice a year, so a later release legitimately returns more records; and the two queries may not be identical — the frozen snapshot of this course was built from a query over IC50, Ki and Kd, while the live call in Section 4 asks only for IC50. What would be wrong is reporting “data from ChEMBL” without the release, query and date, so that the difference could not be attributed to the database rather than to your pipeline. Record the release and the checksum (Unit 2) and the discrepancy becomes information instead of a mystery.

Glossary

Backoff (exponential)
Waiting a doubling interval between retries, with jitter, so that transient failures resolve without overloading a service.
CID / SID
PubChem’s compound (standardised) and substance (as deposited) identifiers.
Columnar format
A layout storing each column contiguously (Parquet), so that reading a subset of columns reads a subset of the file.
DBI
R’s common database interface; RSQLite, RPostgres and duckdb are drivers behind the same functions.
Fixed-column format
A text format in which each field occupies fixed character positions (PDB, SDF atom blocks); parsed with substr(), never by splitting on whitespace.
Foreign key
A column whose values refer to another table’s primary key.
HDF5
A binary container for large, possibly chunked and compressed numeric arrays; read in R through rhdf5.
InChIKey
A 27-character hashed structural identifier: 14-character skeleton block, 10-character stereochemistry/isotope block, one protonation character.
Index (database)
A sorted auxiliary structure turning a table scan into a key lookup; costs storage and write speed. data.table::setkey() is the in-memory analogue.
JSON
A text format for nested data; the standard payload of REST APIs, read in R with jsonlite.
NULL (SQL)
SQL’s marker for an absent value; comparisons with it are never true, exactly as with R’s NA.
Pagination
Returning a large result set in successive pages, each with a pointer to the next.
Parquet
A typed, compressed, columnar file format for tables, read and written in R with arrow.
Primary key
The column (or combination) that uniquely identifies a row.
RDS
R’s own serialisation of a single object; right for caching a fitted model, wrong for exchanging a table.
REST
An architectural style in which resources are addressed by URL and represented, usually, as JSON.
robots.txt
A server-published policy stating which paths automated clients may fetch (RFC 9309).
Row inflation
The multiplication of rows caused by joining on a key that is not unique on one side.
SDF
A multi-record chemical text format carrying atoms, bonds, coordinates and named data fields, terminated by $$$$.
SMILES
A one-line text encoding of a molecular graph.
Subquery
A query used as a table inside another query.

Textbooks

  • Wickham H, Çetinkaya-Rundel M, Grolemund G. R for Data Science. 2nd ed. O’Reilly; 2023. (Free online; the “Import” chapters are the companion reading for Sections 2 and 3.)
  • Beaulieu A. Learning SQL. 3rd ed. O’Reilly; 2020. (Chapters 3–8 cover everything in Section 6 at greater length.)
  • Wickham H. Advanced R. 2nd ed. Chapman and Hall/CRC; 2019. (Free online; the chapter on conditions is the reference for the error handling of Section 4.)

Online resources

  • ChEMBL web-services documentation — the API called in Section 4.
  • ChEMBL downloads — the SQLite and PostgreSQL dumps to use instead of paging an API at scale.
  • httr2, arrow for R, DBI and dbplyr — the four package references for this unit.
  • SQLite documentation and the data.table vignettes on keys and indices.
  • Data Carpentry — the “SQL for ecology/genomics” lessons, which are the same SQL on different data.
